home.title: FerrisGit: a self-hosted Git platform in one Rust binary
home.description: Repositories, merge requests with inline review, issues, wikis, releases, signed webhooks and a built-in CI/CD engine, served by a single Rust binary and one PostgreSQL. Run it with Docker Compose or Helm.

features.title: Product | FerrisGit
features.description: What FerrisGit does today: repositories and groups, merge requests, issues, wikis, releases, CI/CD, mandatory multi-factor authentication, webhooks and public pages. And what is not there yet.

roadmap.title: Roadmap | FerrisGit
roadmap.description: Where FerrisGit is heading, version by version from 0.2 to 0.6: protected branches, five languages, an analysis engine, quality gates, code quality and security analysis. None of it exists yet.

plan.title: Architecture of a FerrisGit instance
plan.description: Isometric drawing. A Git client and a browser talk to one Rust binary, ferrisgit-api, made of the api, application, domain and infrastructure crates. The binary stores its data in PostgreSQL and in Git repositories on disk, and runs pipeline jobs either through a ferrisgit-runner on a Docker host or as Pods in a Kubernetes cluster. An orange line follows a push to its jobs. Seven numbered circles lead to the tiles of the page.
plan.caption: One instance. The orange line follows a push from the client to the jobs it starts.

scene.title: Retry failed webhook deliveries
scene.description: Illustration of one merge request in FerrisGit, from the push to the merge: a push over HTTPS creates the request, a reviewer suggests a change on a line, the author applies it in one click, the reviewer approves, the request is merged. The merge starts the pipeline of the repository: format and clippy run, then test, and all three succeed.
scene.mergeCommit: merge commit, pushed to the default branch

ci.codeLabel: Example of a .ferrisgit-ci.yml for a Rust project: formatting, Clippy and tests
ci.graphLabel: The pipeline of the example file
ci.notePassing: format and clippy start together; test declares needs: [format, clippy] and starts once both have succeeded.
ci.noteFailing: clippy failed: test is skipped without running, because one of the jobs it needs did not succeed. The pipeline ends as failed instead of waiting.

review.title: Review on the diff
review.text: A comment stays attached to its line. A reviewer can write a suggestion that the author applies in one click, as a commit. Approvals are counted, conflicts are detected.
review.comment: Exponential backoff, so a flapping endpoint stops being hammered.

pipeline.title: Pipelines on every push
pipeline.text: After every push, FerrisGit reads the file on the default branch and creates a pipeline. Stages are barriers, needs are dependencies; jobs run in Docker containers through a small runner, or as Kubernetes Pods.

kanban.title: Issues, as a list or a board
kanban.text: Labels, milestones, assignees and four states. Drag a card to change its state, or use the card's menu from the keyboard.
kanban.card1: Pagination skips a page when filtering by label
kanban.card3: Dark mode for the wiki editor

roles.title: Three roles, per repository or per group
roles.text: A role granted on a group applies to everything below it. The highest role wins.

rows.write: Push, open issues and requests, review

webhook.title: Signed webhooks
webhook.text: Twelve events on merge requests, issues, pipelines and collaborators. Each delivery carries an HMAC-SHA256 signature of its raw body; the secret is encrypted at rest.

catalog.title: Public pages, no account needed
catalog.text: Visitors browse the catalogue, README, files, commits and releases of public repositories, and clone them. An administrator switch turns the public pages off.
catalog.repo1: Self-hosted Git platform in Rust: repositories, issues, merge requests and pipelines.
catalog.repo2: Angular design system: components and dataviz for self-hosted applications.

mfa.title: Multi-factor sign-in, for everyone
mfa.text: No account can skip it. Authenticator apps (TOTP), passkeys (WebAuthn) and ten single-use backup codes.

search.title: Search from every page
search.text: Repositories, issues, merge requests and users, as you type. Notifications in the application tell you what concerns you.

regions.compose: Commands to start FerrisGit with Docker Compose

notes.compose: Compose builds the image from the sources. To use the published image instead, replace `build: .` by `image: masmarino/ferrisgit:0.1.1` in `docker-compose.yml`.
notes.helm: Left empty, the chart generates the database password, `JWT_SECRET`, `SETTINGS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and the first administrator's password in the `ferrisgit-secrets` Secret. The release must be called `ferrisgit`.
notes.source: Needs `rustup`, Node.js 26, Docker with Compose and `git` on the PATH. The script starts PostgreSQL, applies the migrations and runs the backend on port 8080 and the Angular dev server on port 4201.

then.title: What happens next
then.secrets: The server refuses to start while a secret is missing or too short: `JWT_SECRET` needs 32 characters or more, `SETTINGS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` exactly 32.
then.start: It connects to PostgreSQL, applies its migrations, creates the first administrator if the users table is empty, and listens on port 8080.
then.signin: The first sign-in walks you through enrolling an authenticator app or a passkey, and shows your ten backup codes. There is no way around it.

needs.title: What you need
needs.docker: Docker with the Compose plugin, or a Kubernetes cluster with Traefik, a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy and a default StorageClass.
needs.postgres: PostgreSQL 18: the Compose stack and the chart bring their own.
needs.https: A domain and TLS in front, through a reverse proxy: FerrisGit does not terminate HTTPS itself, and passkeys only work on a secure origin.

hero.title: A Git platform in one Rust binary.
hero.subtitle: Repositories, merge requests with inline review, issues, wikis, releases, signed webhooks and a CI/CD engine. One process, one PostgreSQL, on your own server.
hero.assurance: A single binary and a database. No account on a third-party service, no telemetry sent anywhere.

binary.label: Rust binary serves the REST API, Git over HTTP and the web interface

postgres.label: PostgreSQL 18 holds every record; repositories live on disk

crates.label: Cargo crates, in a hexagonal layout

mfa.label: sign-in factors (TOTP, passkeys, backup codes); MFA is mandatory

engines.label: job engines: Docker runners or Kubernetes Pods

caps.title: What you get, as the interface shows it
caps.text: Each tile is a piece of the real product. The interface is in French for now; five languages are planned for 0.2.

ci.title: A push becomes a pipeline
ci.text: Describe the jobs in `.ferrisgit-ci.yml` at the root of the repository. After every successful push, FerrisGit reads the file on the default branch and creates a pipeline. Flip the switch to see what the scheduler does when a job fails.

engines.title: Two ways to run a job
engines.text: Docker runners: a small `ferrisgit-runner` binary polls the server and runs each job in a container. Or Kubernetes: the server creates one Pod per job in your cluster.

errors.title: Mistakes are shown
errors.text: A file that is present but invalid creates a failed pipeline that carries the parser's message, shown in the interface.

vars.title: Variables and caches
vars.text: Per-repository CI variables, encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM (Docker runners). Per-job caches with Kubernetes.

install.title: Two minutes to self-host
install.text: FerrisGit is one container image with PostgreSQL next to it. Try it with Docker Compose, install the Helm chart on Kubernetes, or run it from the sources.

made.title: How it is made
made.text: One process, five crates, a hexagonal layout: the domain knows nothing of the database, the adapters know nothing of the use cases.

crates.domain: Entities, value objects and the ports the rest depends on. No I/O.
crates.application: The use cases. Depends on the domain only, tested against in-memory fakes.
crates.infrastructure: Adapters: PostgreSQL (sqlx), Git (gix and the git binary), SMTP, Kubernetes, Argon2, AES-GCM, JWT.
crates.api: The axum server: REST API under /api, Git smart HTTP, the Angular bundle. This is the binary.

security.title: Security and your data
security.text: What protects an instance, named precisely. The data never leaves your server.

mfa.title: Multi-factor authentication is mandatory
mfa.text: An account with no factor enrolled is forced through setup before it can do anything else. TOTP, passkeys and backup codes.

passwords.title: Passwords hashed with Argon2
passwords.text: One salt per password. An unknown username costs as much work as a wrong password, and gets the same answer.

secrets.title: Secrets encrypted with AES-256-GCM
secrets.text: CI variables, webhook secrets, the SMTP password and TOTP secrets, under `SETTINGS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

tokens.title: Tokens for Git, never passwords
tokens.text: Git over HTTPS authenticates with a personal access token, stored hashed: the server cannot read it back.

audit.title: An audit log
audit.text: Failed sign-ins, refused Git access, password resets, promotions and MFA resets by an administrator are recorded as events.

cookies.title: No cookies, strict headers
cookies.text: Sessions are JWTs. Every response carries a Content-Security-Policy, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and the sign-in routes are rate-limited per IP.

data.title: Your data, on your server
data.text: PostgreSQL and a directory of repositories, both yours to back up. The image runs as an unprivileged user on a read-only filesystem.

security.link: The security page of the documentation (in French)

repos.title: Repositories and groups
repos.text: Host code under your own account or inside a hierarchy of groups, and decide who can do what.

bullets.b1: Repositories owned by a user, or nested inside groups and subgroups
bullets.b2: Public or private; the description and the visibility can be changed afterwards
bullets.b3: Reader, Contributor and Maintainer roles, per repository or per group
bullets.b4: Git over HTTP(S): clone, fetch and push with your username and a personal access token

mrs.title: Merge requests
mrs.text: Review happens on the diff, and the whole conversation stays in one place.

bullets.b2: Code suggestions that can be applied from the interface
bullets.b5: A timeline of everything that happened

issues.text: Track the work next to the code.

bullets.b3: A kanban board with four states

bullets.b2: Release files can be downloaded without signing in
bullets.b3: Signed-in users get search, in-app notifications and a personal dashboard

wikis.title: Wikis and releases

bullets.b2: Docker runners (a small `ferrisgit-runner` binary that polls the server) or Kubernetes, where each job runs as a Pod
bullets.b3: Per-repository variables, encrypted at rest (Docker runners only)

bullets.b1: Open to everyone, signed in or not

bullets.b1: Mandatory for every account: authenticator apps (TOTP), passkeys (WebAuthn) and single-use backup codes

roadmap.title: Roadmap: none of this exists yet
roadmap.intro: Versions 0.2 to 0.6, then a list with no order and ideas with no version. The details change as each item is designed.

v02.title: A CI foundation for checks, five languages and a theme setting
v02.intro: Code scanning needs the platform to understand checks: results that belong to a commit, show up on a merge request and can stop a merge. This version builds that, translates the interface and lets people choose its theme.

items.i1: Protected branches: no direct push, merge only through a merge request, required approvals and required checks.
items.i2: Pipelines on merge requests, with their status shown on the merge request and required before a merge.
items.i3: Predefined CI variables (commit, branch, merge request, pipeline) and `rules` to decide when a job runs.
items.i4: Pipeline artifacts and a report upload API, which is what the scans of the next versions use.
items.i5: Re-running a pipeline from the interface, and scheduled pipelines.
items.i6: Personal access tokens usable on the REST API, with scopes, and an OpenAPI description generated from the code.
items.i7: A first link with ArtiFerris: publish an artifact built by a pipeline to an ArtiFerris instance.
items.i8: The interface in English, French, Italian, Spanish and German. The language follows the browser on a first visit, can be changed on the fly and is saved on the account. The e-mails FerrisGit sends use the recipient's language, and the public pages follow the reader's `Accept-Language`. The documentation is translated afterwards.
items.i9: Dark mode as a setting: choose system, light or dark, saved on the account and applied without a flash. The interface follows the system preference today and has no switch. The logo of the signed-in shell follows the theme too.

v03.title: The analysis engine, secrets and dependencies
v03.intro: FerrisGit gets its own analysis engine instead of wrapping third-party tools: a `ferrisgit-scan` binary that a pipeline job runs, so the analysis scales with the runners and the server stays light. Its analysers are plugins that produce findings in a model close to SARIF, so reports from other tools can still be imported next to the native ones.

items.i1: The engine and the findings store: a scan per commit, findings identified by a stable fingerprint, and a baseline per branch to tell the new findings of a merge request from the old ones.
items.i2: Native secret detection, in the diff of a merge request and in the whole history.
items.i3: Native dependency audit: lockfiles (`Cargo.lock`, `package-lock.json`, and others later) matched against public advisory databases such as OSV.
items.i4: Findings shown inline on the merge request diff and summarised in its timeline.
items.i5: Import of SARIF reports from other tools.

items.i1: Quality gates, configurable per repository: for example no new blocker finding and a minimum coverage on new code. A gate is a required check, so it can block a merge.
items.i2: A repository dashboard: open findings, their age, trend per branch, technical debt and hotspots.
items.i3: Triage: mark a finding as a false positive or as won't fix, assign it, suppress it in the code, and keep the history.
items.i4: A `.ferrisgit/scan.yml` file to choose analysers, rule sets and thresholds, and to exclude paths.

v05.title: Code quality
v05.intro: The full repository is analysed on every push to the default branch and on every merge request, and the gates only look at what a merge request introduces (the "clean as you code" approach), so an existing project stays adoptable.

items.i1: Parsing through tree-sitter, so the same engine reads several languages. Rust and TypeScript first.
items.i2: Metrics: size, cyclomatic and cognitive complexity, duplication.
items.i3: Code smells and bug patterns, as declarative rules and as native rules.
items.i4: Test coverage tracking (LCOV and Cobertura reports), with the coverage of what a merge request changes.

items.i1: Static application security testing: pattern rules first, then data flow within a function.
items.i3: A security summary on every merge request and a security dashboard for the repository, with severities and the option to block merging above a chosen severity.
items.i4: Trace every artifact published to ArtiFerris back to the commit, merge request and pipeline that produced it, and show it on the FerrisGit release and pipeline pages.
items.i5: Bring the artifact scan results of ArtiFerris back into the merge request checks.
items.i6: Explore shared identity, so that one account and one MFA enrolment work on both platforms.

platform.title: The platform, in no fixed order

items.i1: Git over SSH and deploy keys.
items.i2: Forks and merge requests between repositories; renaming and transferring a repository with redirects.
items.i3: Squash and rebase merges, reopening a merge request, draft merge requests and `CODEOWNERS`.
items.i4: Mentions (`@name`), issue references (`#12`) and closing an issue from a commit or a merge request.
items.i5: Full-text search in the code, and import from GitHub and GitLab.
items.i6: Self-service password reset, e-mail notifications with per-user settings, and single sign-on (OIDC, LDAP).
items.i7: An audit log page in the administration, Prometheus metrics, and backup and restore tooling.
items.i8: Webhooks with retries, a delivery log and more events (push, release).

consideration.title: Under consideration, not scheduled
consideration.intro: Ideas with no version yet; what they contain is still to be defined.

items.i1: AI agents on a repository. Candidates: a review assistant on merge requests, summaries of merge requests and commits, an explanation of why a pipeline failed, issue triage and labelling. Whatever ships has to fit a self-hosted platform: a model endpoint the administrator chooses (a local one included), opt-in per repository, scoped credentials, and every action recorded.
items.i2: A commit graph in the repository view: branches, merges and tags drawn together, next to the file tree and the commit list that already exist.
items.i3: Profile photos, stored in S3-compatible object storage. The initials stay as the fallback, and the same storage could later hold release files and pipeline artifacts.

artiferris.title: Connecting with ArtiFerris
artiferris.text: ArtiFerris already stores npm packages and Docker/OCI images and scans them for vulnerabilities. FerrisGit and ArtiFerris are complementary halves of the same delivery chain. The link grows in three steps: publishing from a pipeline (0.2), tracing an artifact back to its commit (0.6), and bringing the scan results back into the merge request checks (0.6). Shared identity stays an open question.
